title: Canada Joins UK-Led GCAP Fighter Jet Programme, Signalling Shift Away From US Defence
excerpt: Ottawa becomes the first observer nation in the sixth-generation stealth fighter project developed by Britain, Italy and Japan, as new UK PM Andy Burnham prioritises defence at the Farnborough Airshow.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Canada joins the Global Combat Air Programme as its first observer nation, enhancing military collaboration.
  • New UK PM Andy Burnham signals a strong defense focus with cabinet reshuffles and increased military spending.
  • Canada reduces its F-35 order from 88 to 16 jets, shifting defense procurement away from the US.
  • India may use Canada's observer model as a template for joining GCAP or FCAS in the future.

  • The announcement came on new UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting's first full day in office, as PM Andy Burnham reshuffled his cabinet with a pro-defence tilt.
  • Canada is diversifying defence procurement away from the US, slashing its F-35 order from 88 jets to 16 under PM Mark Carney's strategy.

Canada Steps Into GCAP

Canada has formally joined the Global Combat Air Programme as the first "observer nation," gaining direct access to one of the most ambitious military aviation projects of the 21st century. The announcement, made on Tuesday at the Farnborough Airshow, marks the first expansion of GCAP beyond its three founding members — Britain, Italy and Japan — who launched the programme in 2022 to develop a next-generation stealth fighter by 2035.

Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty, who had discussed the programme with his Japanese counterpart in Tokyo last month, called it a "promising initiative." Observer status grants Canada insight into capability development, industrial collaboration and long-term delivery plans, though it carries no financial commitment.

"This isn't about leverage. The message is, we are stronger together."

— David McGuinty, Canadian Defence Minister
> **"Healey had spent months lobbying for a pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, well above the 2.68% his predecessors had budgeted.

British defence stocks surged."**

The move is part of a broader Canadian strategy to reduce dependence on American arms. Under PM Mark Carney, Ottawa has vowed to stop spending 70% of its defence budget in the United States. Canada slashed its order for Lockheed Martin F-35 jets from 88 to just 16 and is evaluating Swedish-made Gripen E fighters as an alternative.

Burnham's Defence-First Signal

The GCAP announcement was the new British government's first foreign policy move, coming during PM Andy Burnham's opening days in office. Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade, made cabinet moves that sent an unmistakable defence signal to markets.

He appointed John Healey — a former defence secretary who had resigned from Starmer's cabinet over insufficient military spending — as finance minister, and handed the defence portfolio to Wes Streeting. Healey had spent months lobbying for a pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, well above the 2.68% his predecessors had budgeted.

British defence stocks surged. Babcock International climbed 6.8%, Qinetiq gained 4.5% and BAE Systems added 3.1%, outperforming the broader European aerospace and defence index, which rose 1%.

"He understands Rolls-Royce and our agenda and how much we contribute to the country."

— Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO, Rolls-Royce, on John Healey

A Programme Gaining Momentum

GCAP, one of two major Western sixth-generation fighter projects alongside the US Air Force's NGAD programme, received a £4.6 billion ($6.1 billion) contract on 3 July for its advanced concept and assessment phase, running through December 2027. The programme is managed by Edgewing, a joint venture between BAE Systems, Italy's Leonardo and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement.

At the Farnborough Airshow — where defence companies now make up half of a record 1,600 exhibitors — BAE Systems, Boeing and Saab also signed a deal to develop a fast-jet pilot training aircraft based on Boeing's T-7 system, replacing Britain's ageing Hawk fleet.

What It Means for India

Canada's entry into GCAP carries particular significance for India. In March 2026, India's Defence Ministry informed Parliament that the Indian Air Force is seeking to join either GCAP or its European rival, the Franco-German-Spanish Future Combat Air System (FCAS), opening a parallel track alongside India's indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme.

India already has industrial links with GCAP partners. DRDO is collaborating with Rolls-Royce — a key GCAP engine supplier — on the AMCA powerplant. BAE Systems has partnerships with Tata Advanced Systems and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. Canada's observer model, which requires no immediate financial outlay but opens the door to deeper participation, could serve as a template for India's engagement.

What's Next

For Canada, observer status is a stepping stone. Full membership would mean sharing GCAP's billion-dollar development costs and potentially ordering the finished jets. For the UK, the expansion validates Burnham's defence-forward posture as European allies race to reduce dependence on American military hardware. India will weigh whether GCAP or FCAS better serves its sixth-generation ambitions — a decision that could reshape Asia's air combat landscape for decades.
